# Discussion

The analysis of nonlinear effects with latent variables requires estimation procedures that yield reliable results for inference and hypothesis testing. Most approaches rely on distributional assumptions to certain degree. However, these assumptions are frequently violated in applied research. The present study compared the recently proposed LSAM and other estimation methods across two simulation studies, assessing their performance under varying distributional conditions and levels of model complexity.

## Relation to previous findings 

Results across both simulations aligned with prior research. All methods performed adequately under normality. Under non-normal and uniform conditions, LMS and QML exhibited biased estimates for most nonlinear effects, while LSAM and UPI remained relatively unbiased. The efficiency advantage of LMS and QML under non-normality was offset by inflated Type I error rates and reduced coverage when assumptions were violated.

Except under low reliability conditions, LSAM performed adequately across all metrics. Bias results were comparable to 2SMM results reported by @brandt_etall_2014, with largely unbiased estimates across conditions. LMS and QML showed a positive bias for the interaction effect and a negative bias for the quadratic effects under non-normal distributions, consistent with @brandt_etall_2014. Under uniform settings, interaction terms remained unbiased [@lonati_etall_2024] while quadratic effects were biased. UPI also produced unbiased estimates, aligning with earlier results [@brandt_etall_2014; @marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012]. As observed by @brandt_etall_2020, bias increased substantially across all methods under low reliability, although structural misspecifications were not manipulated here. SE/SD ratio results mirrored @brandt_etall_2014, with LMS and QML showing higher efficiency. Type I error rates were generally controlled for the LSAM, whereas the LMS and QML showed an inflation the under non-normal condition as in @brandt_etall_2014. For UPI, type I error rates were not inflated consistent with @marsh_etall_2004 and @cham_etall_2012, despite @brandt_etall_2014 claiming otherwise. The LSAM and UPI also maintained a more stable performance compared to LMS and QML when it comes to coverage under non-normal conditions. To the best of our knowledge, this was the first study to examine coverage directly. For statistical power, LSAM achieved levels at or above 80% only with medium or high reliability under large samples; UPI displayed a similar pattern. LMS and QML reached power above 80% even under low reliability, as in @brandt_etall_2014, but these results must be interpreted cautiously given their inflated type I error rates.

Moreover, these results reinforce that estimator performance depends critically on the number and configuration of nonlinear effects. @lonati_etall_2024 found unbiased LMS estimates for a single interaction under uniform distributions, whereas including quadratic effects in the current study led to substantial bias. This extends @brandt_etall_2014, who also observed deteriorating performance as nonlinear effects increased, underscoring existing estimators' sensitivity to model complexity and distributional violations. Recent developments contextualize these findings. Improved UPI accessibility and ongoing LMS and QML development in open-source software [@kjell_etall_2024], plus LSAM implementation in lavaan [@R-lavaan], represent important advances. New package implementations extend QML and LMS estimation to handle interactions between endogenous and exogenous latent variables, and among endogenous variables, despite persisting limitations. Earlier PI implementations required manually defining numerous parameter constraints, a process prone to error. These developments highlight opportunities for broader adoption and the need for continued caution regarding estimator assumptions and boundary conditions.

## Limitations and Future Research

As with any simulation study, the present findings are conditional on the specific design factors and assumptions examined. The simulations assumed that non-normality in the indicators arose solely from the latent predictor variables. In practice, non-normality may also involve measurement errors or other structural components. Moreover, the sample sizes investigated do not include very small samples that are sometimes encountered in applied research, which may further limit generalization. We also solely focused on distributional violations and did not address structural misspecifications. The robustness of the examined estimators to these additional forms of misspecification remains an important topic for future research.

Furthermore, the literature has mainly relied on robust standard errors and minor methodological modifications to improve estimation under non-normality. For instance, reliability-corrected single-indicator LMS approaches [@cheung_lau_2017; @su_etall_2019] were proposed to reduce sensitivity to distributional violations, although @lonati_etall_2024 found notable gains primarily in small samples. Other studies have explored different ways to form product indicators [@marsh_etall_2004] and compared Wald z-tests with likelihood ratio tests in terms of Type I error and power [@cham_etall_2012], as these are only asymptotically equivalent [@buse_1982]. Robust ML estimators, such as MLR, retain ML parameter estimates but replace normal-theory standard errors with Huber–White sandwich estimators and often apply Yuan–Bentler or Satorra–Bentler corrections to the chi-square statistic. However, these adjustments differ—some affect only standard errors, while others also modify test statistics [@savalei_rosseel_2021]—and simulation evidence suggests that they provide limited improvements [@brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012; @lonati_etall_2024], particularly in small samples. In our study, we relied on standard implementations for the main analyses, and supplementary analyses using robust standard errors showed no substantial improvements. Last, other approaches were not explored [@bollen_1995; @boker_etall_2023; @kelava_etall_2014], some due to limited software implementations availability [@mooijaart_bentler_2010; @kelava_etall_2014].

Concerning a few estimation choices, bounded estimation procedures may enhance UPI performance in smaller samples [@de_jonckere_rosseel_2022], and future work could examine whether alpha correction procedures or separating measurement blocks within models improves estimation for nonlinear and quadratic terms under the LSAM [@rosseel_etall_2025; @rosseel_loh_2024]. Last, the QML estimation can still yield biased results if such models are not appropriately partitioned, as acknowledged in modsem, and indeed it was the case for simulation 2.
